title: Fall Armyworm
summary: A caterpillar that hides in the maize whorl and chews ragged holes in young leaves; the most serious maize pest in Timor-Leste.
symptoms: Ragged holes and windows in young leaves
Sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the whorl
Caterpillars up to 4 cm with an inverted Y on the head and four dots in a square on the last segment
Damaged tassels and bored cobs later in the season
causes: Moths lay eggs on maize leaves; larvae feed for 2–3 weeks
Continuous maize planting keeps the pest cycle going
Warm weather with a green crop available
prevention: Plant early and at the same time as neighbours to avoid staggered food supply
Intercrop maize with beans or plant push-pull companion plants where available
Encourage natural enemies: birds, wasps, ants and earwigs
Scout the field twice a week from emergence to 6 weeks
actions: Check plants early in the morning; hand-pick and crush larvae in the whorl
Apply a pinch of sand, ash or soil into the whorl to dislodge small larvae
Remove and destroy heavily infested plants if damage is over 20%
Ask your extension officer about locally approved biological or chemical options; follow label rates exactly

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Ragged holes in young leaves and sawdust-like frass in the whorl. Look for caterpillars with an inverted Y on the head.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Scout early in the morning, hand-pick larvae, put ash or sand in the whorl, and seek advice on approved treatments if damage is severe.

title: Maize Stem Borer
summary: Larvae tunnel inside the stem, weakening the plant so it snaps or lodges and produces small cobs.
symptoms: Rows of small holes across young leaves (pin-holes and windows)
Dead heart: the central leaf dies in young plants
Holes in the stem with sawdust-like frass pushed out
Plants break or fall over in wind
causes: Moths lay eggs on leaves; larvae bore into the stem
Old maize stalks left in the field over the dry season
prevention: Chop and bury or burn old stalks after harvest
Plant early in the season
Intercrop with beans; the mixed crop confuses the moths
actions: Remove and destroy plants with dead heart
Split damaged stems and kill the larvae
Seek advice on approved treatments if more than 1 in 10 plants are damaged

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Pin-holes across leaves, dead central leaf in young plants, and frass pushed out of stem holes.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Destroy plants with dead heart, clear old stalks after harvest, and seek advice if damage is widespread.

title: Aphids
summary: Tiny soft green or black insects clustered on new shoots and under leaves; they suck sap, curl leaves and spread viruses.
symptoms: Clusters of tiny green, black or grey insects on shoots and under leaves
Curled, sticky or shiny leaves (honeydew) and black sooty mould
Stunted, twisted new growth
Ants running up and down the plant
causes: Warm dry weather and soft new growth from too much nitrogen
Few natural enemies early in the season
prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser
Keep flowering plants nearby to attract ladybirds and hoverflies
Check under leaves weekly
actions: Spray a strong jet of water to knock aphids off
Squash small colonies by hand
Use a mild soap-water spray (about 1 tablespoon of soap in 1 litre of water) on the undersides of leaves; test on a few leaves first
Encourage ladybirds; avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill them

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Tiny insects clustered on shoots and under leaves, curled sticky leaves and ants.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Knock off with water, squash colonies, use soap-water spray, and protect ladybirds.

title: Rice Stem Borer
summary: Larvae bore into rice stems causing dead hearts in young plants and white heads (empty panicles) later.
symptoms: Dead heart: central shoot dries and pulls out easily in the tillering stage
White head: panicle turns white and empty and pulls out easily
Small holes at the base of the stem with frass
causes: Moths lay egg masses on leaves; larvae bore into the stem
Stubble and straw left in the field between crops
prevention: Plough in or remove stubble soon after harvest
Plant at the same time as neighbours
Avoid excess nitrogen
Hand-collect egg masses in the nursery
actions: Pull out and destroy dead hearts and white heads
Cut stubble low at harvest
Seek advice on approved treatments if more than 5% of tillers are affected

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Dead central shoot in young plants and white empty panicles later, both pulling out easily.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Destroy affected tillers, clear stubble after harvest and seek advice if damage exceeds 5% of tillers.

title: Brown Planthopper
summary: Small brown hoppers at the base of rice plants suck sap and cause circular patches of dried, burnt-looking plants (hopperburn).
symptoms: Small brown insects at the base of the stems, jumping when disturbed
Plants yellow then dry out in circular patches
Sooty mould on lower leaves
causes: Continuous flooding and no natural enemies after insecticide use
prevention: Use resistant varieties
Reduce nitrogen and plant at wider spacing
Drain the field for 3–4 days to disturb the hoppers
Protect spiders and other natural enemies
actions: Drain the field temporarily
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that trigger outbreaks
Seek advice quickly if hopperburn patches appear

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Brown hoppers at the stem base and circular patches of dried, burnt-looking rice.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Drain the field briefly, reduce nitrogen, protect natural enemies and seek advice quickly.

title: Whitefly
summary: Tiny white flies under tomato and chili leaves that fly up in clouds when disturbed; they weaken plants and spread leaf-curl virus.
symptoms: Clouds of tiny white insects rising when leaves are shaken
Yellowing, curling leaves and sticky honeydew
Stunted plants with curled, yellow-edged young leaves (virus)
causes: Warm dry weather and nearby infested crops or weeds
Seedlings already infested in the nursery
prevention: Cover nursery beds with fine net
Remove weeds and old crops around the field
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers
actions: Remove and destroy virus-affected plants early
Spray soap-water on the undersides of leaves in the early morning
Seek advice on approved treatments if numbers keep rising

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Tiny white insects flying up from under leaves; leaves curl and yellow.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove virus-affected plants, use sticky traps, spray soap-water under leaves and seek advice if numbers rise.

title: Tomato Fruit Borer
summary: A caterpillar that bores holes into tomato and chili fruit, leaving them rotten inside.
symptoms: Round holes in fruit, often with the caterpillar's rear end sticking out
Fruit rots around the hole
Chewed flowers and buds
causes: Moths lay eggs on flowers and young fruit
Warm weather and continuous host crops
prevention: Hand-pick caterpillars and eggs on flowers
Remove and destroy damaged fruit promptly
Encourage birds and wasps
actions: Collect and bury damaged fruit twice a week
Hand-pick caterpillars in the evening
Seek advice on approved biological sprays (e.g. Bt) if damage is high

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Round holes in fruit with rot inside; chewed flowers.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove damaged fruit, hand-pick caterpillars in the evening and seek advice on biological sprays if needed.

title: Maize Weevils in Storage
summary: Small beetles that bore into stored maize grain, turning it to powder within months if not controlled.
symptoms: Small round holes in kernels
Flour-like dust in stored grain
Small brown beetles with a long snout walking on the grain
causes: Grain stored before it is fully dry
Open bags or baskets that let beetles in
Old infested grain kept near new harvest
prevention: Dry grain until a kernel cracks when bitten (about 13% moisture)
Store in sealed drums, jerry cans or hermetic bags
Clean the store and remove old grain before the new harvest
actions: Sun-dry infested grain for 2–3 days and sieve out the beetles
Move clean grain to a sealed container immediately
Do not use chemicals not approved for food storage

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Round holes in kernels, floury dust and small snouted beetles in stored maize.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Dry grain fully, sieve out beetles, and store in sealed drums or hermetic bags.
